about: Bio English Lab, public: the labs' glossary-only cards and each card's Cambridge Dictionary UK/US recording addresses (played from dictionary.cambridge.org), for My assessments.

g.abdomen.d: The rear part of an arthropod’s body, behind the thorax or cephalothorax.

g.actual_size.d: The real length of a specimen, not of its image. Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. Give it with its unit, usually millimetres (mm).

g.adhesion.d: Water holding on to a surface: hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the polar cellulose of the xylem walls, which keep the column against the wall so it does not slip back.

g.toxin.d: A poisonous substance. Some pathogens produce toxins: the toxin of the cholera bacterium causes secretion of chloride ions into the small intestine. Some toxins can pass across the placenta and affect the fetus.

g.diarrhoea.d: The loss of large volumes of watery faeces. In cholera, water moves into the gut by osmosis, causing diarrhoea.

g.dehydration.d: The loss of too much water from the body. In cholera, diarrhoea causes dehydration and loss of ions from the blood.

g.apical_meristem.d: The region of dividing cells at the very tip of a shoot, and at the tip of a root just behind the root cap. It makes the new cells; those cells then lengthen in the zone just behind it, and that lengthening adds most of the extra length. The 0610 syllabus does not name it, but an exam question can still use it.

g.alga.d: A protoctist that photosynthesises: a single cell, or a simple many-celled body such as a seaweed, with chloroplasts and a cell wall but no true roots, stems or leaves.

g.anaemia.d: Anaemia is the condition in which the blood carries too little haemoglobin, so it carries less oxygen and the person feels tired and weak. In the diet, the usual cause is too little iron, which is needed to make haemoglobin.

g.anatomy.d: The internal structure of an organism — the parts inside it and how they are arranged. Classification once rested on anatomy and morphology; DNA now settles the arguments those could not.

g.antenna.d: A jointed feeler on the head of an arthropod, sensing touch and chemicals. Plural: antennae. Insects and myriapods have one pair, crustaceans two, arachnids none.

g.anus.d: The opening at the end of the alimentary canal through which faeces are egested.

g.associated_organ.d: An organ that secretes into the alimentary canal but that food never passes through: the salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gall bladder.

g.autotrophic_nutrition.d: Making your own organic substances (food) from simple inorganic ones. In plants and the algae this is photosynthesis: carbon dioxide and water are built into glucose using energy from light. An organism that feeds this way is an autotroph.

g.backbone.d: The column of small units (vertebrae) along the back of a vertebrate, around the nerve cord. They are bone in most vertebrates and cartilage in sharks and rays.

g.base.d: One of the four units — A, T, C and G — whose order along a DNA strand carries the genetic information.

g.base_sequence.d: The order of the bases along a stretch of DNA. Organisms that share a more recent common ancestor have more similar base sequences.

g.bile_duct.d: The bile duct is the tube that carries bile into the duodenum. Strictly it is the common bile duct: it receives bile from the gall bladder (through the cystic duct) and bile coming straight from the liver (through the hepatic ducts).

g.blood_vessel.d: A tube that carries blood: an artery, a vein or a capillary.

g.bolus.d: The ball of chewed food, mixed with saliva, produced by mastication and ready to be swallowed. It becomes chyme once the stomach has churned it.

g.cambium.d: A single layer of dividing cells between the xylem and the phloem of a stem or root. In a tree it makes new xylem — wood — on its inside each year, and new phloem on its outside; each year’s xylem is one annual ring.

g.canine.d: A long, sharp, pointed tooth used to hold and tear at food.

g.capsule.d: A slimy layer outside the cell wall of many bacteria. It protects the cell.

g.carbohydrase.d: The general name for enzymes that break carbohydrates down into simple sugars.

g.catabolic.d: Describes a reaction, or an enzyme, that breaks a larger molecule into smaller ones. Digestion is catabolic throughout. The opposite is anabolic: building a larger molecule from smaller ones.

g.cell_elongation.d: Cells getting longer, which is how a shoot grows in length. Auxin stimulates it.

g.cell_sap.d: The solution of sugars and salts in water inside the large permanent vacuole of a plant cell.

g.circular_dna.d: The loop of DNA that carries a bacterium's genes. It lies free in the cytoplasm, because a bacterium has no nucleus.

g.connective_tissue.d: A tissue that supports other tissues and holds them together: a few scattered cells among the fibres they make.

g.coverslip.d: A very thin square of glass laid over a specimen on a slide. It keeps the specimen flat and stops it drying out.

g.deoxygenated.d: Carrying little oxygen, because it has given oxygen to respiring cells. Drawn blue on diagrams, although real deoxygenated blood is dark red.

g.elastic_fibres.d: Fibres in the wall of an artery that stretch when a surge of blood arrives and recoil between beats, which keeps the blood moving and evens out the pressure.

g.electrical_impulse.d: The signal that travels along a neurone. Electrical impulses carry information through the nervous system.

g.flagellum.d: A long, thin thread that moves a cell. A sperm cell swims with its flagellum, and many bacteria have flagella.

g.genetic_predisposition.d: An inherited greater chance of developing a disease, often seen as a family history of it.

g.gill.d: A gas exchange organ of a fish. Blood flowing through its capillaries absorbs oxygen from the water that flows over it.

g.heart_rate.d: The number of times the heart beats in one minute, in beats per minute (bpm).

g.image_size.d: The length of a specimen in a drawing or a photograph, measured with a ruler, in millimetres (mm).

g.light_microscope.d: An instrument that passes light through a thin specimen and magnifies it with two lenses: the objective lens, near the specimen, and the eyepiece lens, near the eye. Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.

g.muscle_tissue.d: A tissue of cells that contract. In the wall of the uterus or of the gut it squeezes what is inside; in the heart it pumps the blood.

g.oxygenated.d: Carrying a lot of oxygen, combined with haemoglobin — like blood that has just passed through the lungs. Drawn red on diagrams.

g.photomicrograph.d: A photograph taken through a microscope. Its magnification, or a scale bar, is printed beside it.

g.physical_activity.d: Movement that makes the muscles work harder than at rest, such as walking, running or cycling.

g.pulmonary_circulation.d: The part of a double circulation that carries blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side.

g.risk_factor.d: Something that makes a disease more likely, without always causing it. For coronary heart disease: diet, lack of exercise, stress, smoking, genetic predisposition, age and sex.

g.scale_bar.d: A line on a photograph or a drawing, labelled with the real length it stands for, such as 10 µm. Compare the specimen with it to find the actual size.

g.slide.d: A thin rectangle of glass on which a specimen is put, to be looked at with a microscope.

g.stain.d: A coloured dye that makes some parts of a cell easier to see. Methylene blue stains the nucleus of an animal cell.

g.stethoscope.d: An instrument for listening to sounds inside the body, such as the heart valves closing.

g.systemic_circulation.d: The part of a double circulation that carries blood from the left side of the heart to the rest of the body and back to the right side.

g.cement.d: The thin, bone-like layer covering the root of a tooth that helps anchor it to the jawbone.

g.cephalothorax.d: The front part of the body of an arachnid or a crustacean: the head and thorax fused into one, carrying the legs.

g.characteristic.d: One of the seven processes that living organisms carry out — movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition. Every kind of living organism shows all seven, so naming a characteristic never picks out a group on its own; that is what a feature does. The way a characteristic is carried out can differ, and nutrition is the example: autotrophic in plants, heterotrophic in animals and fungi.

g.chitin.d: The tough material a fungal cell wall is made of — and the same material as an arthropod’s exoskeleton. It is not cellulose, which is what a plant cell wall is made of.

g.chyme.d: The acidic, soupy mixture of partly digested food and gastric juice that leaves the stomach and enters the duodenum. It was a bolus before the stomach churned it.

g.circular_folds.d: Circular folds are ridges running round the inside of the small intestine that roughly triple the surface area compared with a flat tube.

g.circular_muscle.d: A ring of muscle in the wall of the alimentary canal; when it contracts, the tube becomes narrower. It is the circular muscle that contracts behind the bolus in peristalsis, squeezing it forwards — so this is the muscle to name.

g.cohesion.d: Water holding on to water: hydrogen bonds between water molecules, which make the water in the xylem one continuous column, so a pull at the top moves the whole of it. The syllabus calls it forces of attraction between water molecules.

g.coleoptile.d: The hollow sheath that covers the first shoot of a grass seedling — oat, maize, wheat — as it pushes up through the soil, protecting the folded first leaf inside. Its tip makes the auxin and detects the light. The classic auxin experiments were all done on coleoptiles, because a coleoptile is a straight hollow tube with no leaves in the way: you can cut the tip off, put it back, cap it, or slide a barrier into it. 0610 asks only for the shoot tip.

g.colon.d: The main part of the large intestine, which reabsorbs water and mineral ions from undigested material.

g.common_ancestor.d: An organism from which two or more groups are descended. The more recent the common ancestor, the more closely related the groups.

g.complementary.d: Matching in shape, like a key to a lock. An enzyme's active site is complementary to its substrate: the two fit together, and no other molecule does.

g.compound_eye.d: An eye made of many small lenses, each facing a slightly different way. Insects and crustaceans have them; arachnids have simple eyes instead.

g.concentration.d: How much of a substance there is in a given volume. A concentrated solution has a lot of it dissolved in a little water; a dilute solution has a little in a lot of water.

g.condensation.d: The reverse of hydrolysis: two molecules are joined and a molecule of water is released. It is how the body builds glycogen from glucose and proteins from amino acids — the reaction that digestion undoes.

g.constipation.d: Hard, difficult-to-pass faeces, caused when material moves slowly through the colon and too much water is reabsorbed.

g.consumed.d: Used up. A catalyst is not consumed in the reaction it speeds up: it is still there, unchanged, at the end, and can be used again.

g.control.d: A part of an experiment set up in the same way as the test but with the one factor being investigated left out or held fixed, so that any difference in the result can be put down to that factor and to nothing else.

g.cotyledon.d: A seed leaf: the leaf, or pair of leaves, already formed inside a seed. Monocotyledons have one, dicotyledons two.

g.de_starching.d: Keeping a plant in the dark for about two days, so that its leaves use up their stored starch. Any starch found afterwards was made during the experiment.

g.deficiency_disease.d: A disease caused by not having enough of a particular nutrient in the diet.

g.denatured.d: Describes an enzyme whose active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme stops working. For 0610, treat the change as permanent: cooling a heat-denatured enzyme does not bring it back, and an enzyme is never 'killed', because it was never alive. (In reality some denaturation is reversible — a gently unfolded protein can refold — but that is not the answer 0610 asks for.)

g.dentine.d: Dentine is the bone-like layer beneath the enamel that makes up most of a tooth. It is softer than enamel and is crossed by tiny tubules running out from the living cells of the pulp, which is why a tooth with worn enamel feels cold and pain.

g.dry_mass.d: The mass of an organism with all the water removed: what is left is the material it has made, so an increase in dry mass is real growth.

g.ectotherm.d: An animal whose body temperature follows the temperature of its surroundings — reptiles, amphibians and fish. It warms up by moving into the sun and cools by moving into shade, so it needs far less food than an endotherm of the same size. The older word is cold-blooded, which is misleading: a lizard in the sun is warmer than you are.

g.enamel.d: The hard outer layer of a tooth, made of calcium salts; it is the hardest substance in the body and protects the tooth from wear and acid.

g.endotherm.d: An animal that keeps a constant body temperature using heat released by its own metabolism — mammals and birds. It stays active in the cold, and pays for it: an endotherm needs several times the food an ectotherm of the same size needs. The older word is warm-blooded.

g.enterocyte.d: An enterocyte is one of the epithelial cells lining a villus: a tall cell with microvilli on its top surface and many mitochondria, built for absorbing digested food.

g.epiglottis.d: A flap of cartilage that folds down over the opening of the trachea during swallowing so that food enters the oesophagus.

g.epithelium.d: An epithelium is a tissue: a sheet of closely packed cells that covers a surface or lines a tube or cavity — skin, the airways and the gut all have one. In the small intestine it is the single layer of cells (enterocytes) covering each villus, through which food molecules are absorbed.

g.equilibrium.d: The state reached when there is no longer any net movement, because the concentrations on both sides are equal. The particles are still moving; they are simply moving both ways equally.

g.evolutionary_relationships.d: How closely organisms are related by descent from common ancestors. Classification systems aim to reflect them.

g.exoskeleton.d: A hard skeleton on the outside of the body, as in arthropods. It cannot grow, so the animal moults.

g.external_fertilisation.d: Fertilisation outside the body, usually in water, as in fish and amphibians.

g.fats_and_oils.d: Fats and oils (lipids) are nutrients built from glycerol and fatty acids. They store energy, insulate the body and protect organs; butter, oils, nuts and oily fish are rich in them.

g.feature.d: Something an organism has, or does, that can be observed and used to place it in a group — feathers, jointed legs, a cell wall, seeds in a cone. Classification uses features. Habitat and behaviour are not features. Keep it apart from characteristic: the seven characteristics are the processes every living organism carries out.

g.fertile_offspring.d: Offspring that can themselves reproduce. Two organisms belong to one species if they can breed and their offspring are fertile — most ligers (the cubs of a lion and a tiger) are not, so lions and tigers are separate species.

g.fibrous_root_system.d: Many roots of about the same thickness spreading out from the base of the stem, with no single main root. Monocotyledons have one.

g.flowering_plant.d: A plant that reproduces by flowers, with seeds formed inside an ovary. Two groups: monocotyledons and dicotyledons.

g.frond.d: The leaf of a fern, usually divided into many leaflets and unrolling from a coil as it grows.

g.gum.d: The soft tissue that covers the jawbone and seals around the neck of each tooth; it needs vitamin C to stay healthy.

g.heterotrophic_nutrition.d: Taking in organic substances made by other organisms, and breaking them down to be absorbed and used. Animals, fungi and many prokaryotes and protoctists feed this way; each is a heterotroph.

g.holozoic_nutrition.d: The heterotrophic nutrition of most animals: food is taken into the body, digested inside it, and the products absorbed. Fungi do the opposite — they digest outside and absorb after.

g.host_cell.d: A living cell that a virus enters and uses to make copies of itself.

g.hydrolysis.d: A reaction in which a bond is broken by adding a molecule of water. Every digestive reaction is a hydrolysis: starch to maltose, protein to amino acids, fat to fatty acids and glycerol. The enzymes that catalyse it are called hydrolases.

g.hypha.d: One of the fine threads that make up the body of most fungi. Plural: hyphae; the mass of them is the mycelium.

g.incisor.d: A chisel-shaped tooth at the front of the mouth, used for cutting and biting off pieces of food.

g.insoluble.d: Not able to dissolve. Starch, protein and fat are insoluble, which is why they have to be digested into soluble molecules before they can be absorbed.

g.internal_fertilisation.d: Fertilisation inside the body of the female, as in mammals, birds and reptiles.

g.iodine_solution.d: The test for starch: orange-brown, it turns blue-black where starch is present.

g.jawbone.d: The bone in which the roots of the teeth are set, holding each tooth in its socket.

g.longitudinal_muscle.d: Muscle running along the length of the wall of the alimentary canal; when it contracts, the tube becomes shorter and wider. It works in alternation with the circular muscle, but peristalsis answers are marked on the circular muscle.

g.magnesium_ion.d: A mineral ion taken in through the roots and used to make chlorophyll. (Too little, and the leaves turn yellow.)

g.malnutrition.d: The result of a diet that is not balanced — too little, too much, or the wrong proportions.

g.mammary_glands.d: The glands of a female mammal that make milk for the young.

g.mastication.d: The cutting and mixing of food with saliva by the teeth and tongue.

g.mesophyll.d: The photosynthesising tissue inside a leaf, between the upper and lower epidermis: the palisade layer above and the spongy layer below.

g.model.d: A simplified stand-in for something that cannot easily be studied directly, used because it can be set up and measured in a laboratory. A model is judged by what it explains, and every model has limits — the places where it stops behaving like the real thing.

g.molar.d: A large, broad tooth at the back of the mouth used for chewing and grinding hard food.

g.monomer.d: A small molecule (a sub-unit) that joins with others to build a polymer — glucose is the monomer of starch, glycogen and cellulose; an amino acid is the monomer of protein.

g.morphology.d: The form and shape of an organism — the visible structure biologists used to classify organisms before DNA sequences.

g.mycelium.d: The mass of hyphae that forms the body of a fungus, usually hidden in the soil or in what it feeds on.

g.negative_control.d: A control set up so that it should give a negative result, because whatever is being tested for has been deliberately left out. If it gives a positive result instead, the apparatus, the reagents or the method is at fault, and the rest of the results cannot be trusted.

g.net_movement.d: The overall movement once movement in both directions is counted. Particles move about at random in every direction; when more go one way than the other, the net movement is that way. It is what diffusion describes, and it stops when the concentrations are equal — the particles keep moving, but there is no longer a net movement.

g.neutralise.d: To cancel out an acid using an alkali, raising the pH towards neutral or slightly alkaline.

g.nitrate_ion.d: A mineral ion taken in through the roots and used to make amino acids, and so proteins. (Too little, and growth is stunted and the leaves turn pale.)

g.optimum.d: The value at which something works best. An enzyme's optimum temperature and optimum pH are the ones at which it works fastest; away from them it works more slowly, and far from them it is denatured.

g.ovary.d: In a flower, the swollen base of the carpel that holds the ovules; after fertilisation it becomes the fruit and the ovules become the seeds. In an animal, the organ that makes egg cells.

g.pancreatic_juice.d: The alkaline fluid the pancreas secretes into the duodenum; it contains amylase, protease (trypsin) and lipase.

g.parasite.d: An organism that lives on or in another organism, its host, taking food from it and doing it harm. Parasites are found in several groups: animals such as the tapeworm and the flea, protoctists such as the malaria parasite, and many fungi.

g.parasitic_nutrition.d: Heterotrophic nutrition in which an organism (the parasite) feeds on or in a living host, harming it. Plasmodium, which causes malaria, feeds this way.

g.partially_permeable.d: Describes a membrane that lets some substances through but not others, usually according to the size of the molecule. The membrane of every cell is partially permeable, and so is the wall of the small intestine.

g.periodontal_fibres.d: Tough fibres between the cement and the jawbone that hold the tooth firmly in its socket and act as shock absorbers. The 0610 syllabus does not name it, but an exam question can still use it.

g.pharynx.d: The space at the back of the mouth and nose where the path of food and the path of air cross.

g.phylum.d: The rank below kingdom: a kingdom is divided into phyla, a phylum into classes, and so on down through order, family and genus to species. The arthropods are one phylum of the animal kingdom.

g.plumule.d: The embryo shoot inside a seed, which grows up after the radicle.

g.polymer.d: A large molecule made of many small sub-units (monomers) joined into a chain. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polymers of glucose; a protein is a polymer of amino acids.

g.positive_control.d: A control set up so that it must give a positive result, because whatever is being tested for is known to be present. If it comes out negative, the test or the apparatus is not working, so a negative result anywhere else in the experiment would prove nothing either.

g.premolar.d: A tooth with a ridged surface used to crush and grind soft food.

g.protein_coat.d: The layer of protein around the genetic material of a virus.

g.pulp.d: The pulp is the soft, living tissue in the centre of a tooth (filling the pulp cavity): blood vessels that supply the tooth, and nerves that detect pain, heat and cold.

g.radicle.d: The embryo root inside a seed: the first part to grow out at germination.

g.reabsorbed.d: Absorbed back into the blood after having been released into the gut. Most of the water in the digestive juices is reabsorbed in the small intestine and the colon.

g.root_canal.d: The channel running down the root of a tooth along which the blood vessels and nerves reach the pulp cavity. The 0610 syllabus does not name it, but an exam question can still use it.

g.root_cortex.d: The layer of cells in a root between the epidermis and the xylem, which water crosses from cell to cell on its way in from the root hairs.

g.saliva.d: Saliva is the watery fluid the salivary glands secrete into the mouth. It contains mucus, which lubricates the food, and the enzyme salivary amylase, which begins the digestion of starch.

g.salivary_amylase.d: The carbohydrase enzyme in saliva that breaks starch down into maltose.

g.saprotrophic_nutrition.d: Feeding on dead organic material by releasing enzymes onto it and absorbing the digested products. How most fungi feed.

g.secrete.d: To release a useful substance made by a gland or cell. The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum; secreting is not the same as excreting, which is getting rid of waste.

g.seedling.d: The young plant that grows from a seed: the radicle has become its first root and the plumule its first shoot. Until its leaves have opened it lives on the food stored in the seed.

g.shoot_tip.d: The growing end of a shoot, where auxin is made.

g.soluble.d: Able to dissolve in a liquid, usually water. Small food molecules such as glucose and amino acids are soluble, which is why they can be carried in the blood and cross the wall of the intestine.

g.specimen.d: The actual organism, or part of one, in front of you — the thing you observe and draw.

g.spore.d: A tiny reproductive cell that can grow into a new organism on its own, made by ferns and fungi.

g.swallowing.d: The reflex that pushes the bolus from the mouth, through the pharynx, into the oesophagus.

g.tap_root.d: One main root growing straight down with smaller roots branching from it. Dicotyledons have one.

g.taxonomy.d: The science of classifying and naming organisms. The groups are called taxa; the ranks run kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

g.testa.d: The seed coat: the tough protective covering of a seed, softened and split by water at germination.

g.transpiration_stream.d: The movement of water from the roots, up the xylem, to the leaves. The stream is the movement; the force that drives it is the transpiration pull.

g.triglyceride.d: A lipid (a fat or an oil) made of one molecule of glycerol joined to three fatty acids — which is what digestion by lipase breaks it back into.

g.variegated_leaf.d: A leaf with green parts and white parts. The white parts have no chlorophyll, which is what makes it the test for whether chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

g.succulent.d: A xerophyte with thick, fleshy stems or leaves that hold a store of water, so the plant can live through a dry season. A cactus is one.

g.marram_grass.d: The grass that grows on sand dunes, and the xerophyte the exam uses most: its leaves roll into a tube, with the stomata sunk in pits on the inside.

g.xylem_vessel.d: One of the long, hollow tubes of the xylem: dead cells joined end to end with no cross walls and no cell contents, and thick walls stiffened with lignin.

g.daughter_cell.d: One of the new cells made when a cell divides.

g.genetic_diagram.d: A diagram that predicts the offspring of a cross, line by line: the parents’ phenotypes and genotypes, their gametes, the offspring’s genotypes and phenotypes, and the ratio.

g.phenotypic_ratio.d: The ratio of the phenotypes expected in the offspring of a cross, for example 3 round : 1 wrinkled. It is a likelihood, the expected chance of each phenotype, not a count of the offspring.

g.blood_group.d: One of the four ABO phenotypes in humans: A, B, AB and O. One gene with three alleles, Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᵒ, controls them: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, and both are dominant to Iᵒ.

g.red_green_colour_blindness.d: A sex-linked characteristic: the gene for colour vision is on the X chromosome, and the Y chromosome has no copy of it. A person with no dominant allele, a man XᵇY or a woman XᵇXᵇ, cannot distinguish red from green.

g.genetic_material.d: The material that carries the genes of a cell or a virus: DNA (in some viruses, RNA). In a cell with a nucleus, most of it is in the chromosomes.

g.genome.d: All of the genetic material of an organism, with all of its genes. The human genome is one set of 23 chromosomes; a body cell holds two sets, one from each parent.

g.chromatid.d: One of the two identical copies of a chromosome, made when the chromosome is copied before a cell divides. The two chromatids stay joined at one point, so the chromosome shows as a cross, until they separate. The 0610 syllabus calls them the copies of a chromosome.

g.carrier.d: A person who is heterozygous for a recessive allele that causes a condition: they do not have the condition, but their children can inherit the allele. A woman XᴮXᵇ is a carrier of red-green colour blindness.
